incumbent.text: Reproduce-then-boundary-containment: first reproduce the flaw against a live local handler using a fixture root with a sibling marker file and raw requests carrying literal parent-directory segments, so no client-side normalization hides the behavior. Characterize which shapes leak, including the extensionless index-append branch and deep traversal. Then implement the minimal repair at the path-derivation boundary: after joining, resolve the configured root and the joined target and accept only when the target equals the root or begins with the root plus the path separator; otherwise return the existing 404 page. Close with a regression suite covering ordinary files, nested files, directory index, missing files, and traversal variants. Assumption: the join is the single trust boundary; falsifier: a leaking shape that a resolved-prefix check still admits.

hint: A generic HTTP static-file handler joins the configured content root with the request pathname, appends a default index filename when the joined target has no extension, and streams existing regular files. A minimal repair now resolves the configured root and the joined target and rejects with the existing 404 page unless the target equals the root or begins with the root plus the path separator; the gate is placed before the extensionless append. A 15-case regression run on the patched copy passed all cases, while the vulnerable copy failed exactly the seven traversal cases. Ordinary in-root requests returned 200 with body hashes matching the source files. The patched and vulnerable trees are separate disposable copies; the observer may read and run both, create fixtures, and use ephemeral loopback ports. Remaining work is closure and limitation characterization: query strings, a relative root under a changed working directory, a sibling directory sharing a long name prefix, concurrent requests, and a symlink inside the root pointing outside; then package the repair.
